facts.claim: Kraton Yogyakarta 'Dhaup Ageng' (16 April 2017; re-checked live, HTTP 200): Dhaup Ageng is the ceremony a king holds when marrying off a daughter; in Javanese tradition the wedding is hosted by the bride's side. The page describes the royal procession as practised under Sri Sultan Hamengku Bawono Ka10 and says it has been simplified over time. ROYAL PRACTICE ONLY.

Kraton Yogyakarta: panggih is the meeting of the couple after they are legally married; in the royal version the groom carries 4 rolled betel leaves (gantal) and throws first, slowly, to the bride who carries 3; the bride then washes the groom's feet, followed by breaking an egg. The royal version adds pondongan (the bride lifted to shoulder height by the groom and the bride's uncle) to honour her as a daughter of the Sultan and the queen consort. The page does NOT name the sindur cloth walk, timbang/pangkon or kacar-kucur by those names. ROYAL PRACTICE; do not state counts as universal.
facts.conflicts: Royal counts 4 and 3 gantal; non-royal counts may differ.

facts.claim: Kraton Yogyakarta: after panggih come tampa kaya (the groom pours coins and various grains for the bride to receive, symbolising the husband's responsibility to provide and bring prosperity) and dhahar klimah (shared meal; the groom forms three balls of rice with side dishes and gives them to the bride to eat). ROYAL PRACTICE; these are the palace's names for what are often told as kacar-kucur and dulangan.

Kraton Yogyakarta: after the ijab qobul at the akad nikah, the groom performs sungkeman to the Sultan as a mark of respect and to ask for his blessing. This is the only sungkeman the page names, and it is ROYAL PRACTICE (the groom to the Sultan, after the akad, before panggih); the page does not describe sungkeman to both sets of parents.

Kraton Yogyakarta: after siraman the bride's fine hair on the forehead and nape is shaved (dikerik) to create the cengkorongan, the outline or pattern for the paes ageng make-up. ROYAL PRACTICE; the page does not describe Solo styles.

Kraton Yogyakarta: at the royal reception the palace dances Beksan Bedhaya Manten (Sanghaskara), six unmarried female dancers, two playing the bride and groom, symbolising the couple's journey to married life, and Beksan Lawung Ageng (12 male dancers, a soldiers' dance created by Sultan Hamengku Buwono I) are performed. The page does not name the gamelan pieces played. ROYAL PRACTICE.

UNESCO page title 'Gamelan' (Indonesia), inscribed in 2021 (16.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. UNESCO says gamelan is the traditional Indonesian percussion orchestra and its instruments, 'typically performed in religious rituals, ceremonies, traditional theatre, festivals and concerts'. The text does NOT mention weddings or marriage, so per the brief the article must not say UNESCO links gamelan to weddings (it may say UNESCO lists ceremonies generally).

Widyaparwa 49(1) 2021 (peer-reviewed, Balai Bahasa DIY), Nardilla: studies panyandra, the poetic narration by the master of ceremonies during the panggih ceremony in the Surakarta style (Nganjuk, East Java), with similes and metaphors of beauty and good wishes for the couple. Carried over from the Indonesian pack (checked 2026-11-03), NOT re-fetched in this batch.

ABSTRACT ONLY: Priyatiningsih (Universitas Veteran Bangun Nusantara Sukoharjo), 'Pendidikan Karakter Melalui Tradisi Sungkeman Adat Jawa', Jurnal Sustainable 5(2), 458-462 (published 12 Feb 2023; SINTA 4), DOI 10.32923/kjmp.v5i2.3228. In the wedding rite, sungkeman teaches the child's obedience to both parents, parents-in-law and even grandparents, Javanese etiquette of honouring elders, and asking for blessing (doa restu) for a happy, lasting marriage. Qualitative descriptive study. The abstract does not fix sungkeman's place in the sequence.

Australian Embassy Indonesia 'Marriage in Indonesia' (re-checked live 2026-11-04, HTTP 200): neither DFAT nor its missions can advise on other countries' specific marriage requirements; contact the nearest Indonesian Embassy/Consulate-General or the Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage will take place; the page is a general guide only and suggests discussing further steps with a lawyer in Australia and/or Indonesia.

Embassy page: persons of any nationality may generally marry in Indonesia provided they hold a religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (page lists Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism or Christian); marriages may be performed by ministers of religion, Civil Registry officers (Kantor Catatan Sipil) or the Office of Religious Affairs (KUA); to be legal it must be conducted according to the religion and conform to the laws of the countries of both parties.
Embassy page, 'Couples must be of the same religion': under Indonesian Law No. 1 of 1974 concerning marriage, both parties must hold the same religion; if not, one party must convert.

Embassy page: an Australian marrying in Indonesia applies for a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) at the Australian Embassy Jakarta or the Consulates-General in Denpasar, Surabaya or Makassar. Jurisdiction guide (check with the Civil Registry or KUA): Embassy Jakarta covers Jakarta, West Java and Yogyakarta (among others); Consulate-General Surabaya covers East Java and Central Java; Consulate-General Bali covers Bali, NTB and NTT. CNI usually issued while you wait if documents are complete; no expiry is set but Civil Registry Offices do not normally accept CNIs issued more than 3 months prior. You cannot marry at the Embassy/Consulate-General. No fee is stated on the page.
facts.conflicts: Indonesian pack fact_105 did not record the Java jurisdiction split; new detail: Yogyakarta under Jakarta, Central Java (incl. Solo) under Surabaya.

facts.claim: Embassy page: Muslim weddings are performed by the KUA, which issues the Marriage Book (Buku Nikah); Civil Registry registration usually not required but a Civil Registry marriage certificate is recommended if relocating. Non-Muslim marriages: lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding and register the marriage there after the ceremony for it to be legal. Documents listed: CNI, passports or KTP, birth certificates, marriage certificate, proof of dissolution of a previous marriage or death certificate (if applicable), four 4x6 cm photos; requirements vary by province. The page also notes liaising without Indonesian language skills can be difficult.

Embassy FAQ: since 1 January 1995 any marriage legally performed overseas that would have been legal had it been performed in Australia is accepted as legal under Australian law; no need to register with the Embassy; you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia; you cannot marry before a divorce decree absolute is issued.

Smartraveller Indonesia (re-checked live 2026-11-04; 'Updated: 21 October 2026', 'Still current at: 04 November 2026'): 'Exercise a high degree of caution' in Indonesia overall due to security risks (level 2); 'Reconsider your need to travel' (level 3) to Papua Pegunungan and Papua Tengah. No Java province or Bali is listed in a higher-level area. Missions: Embassy Jakarta; Consulates-General Bali, Makassar, Surabaya. Volcano list includes Mount Merapi (between Central Java and Yogyakarta) and Mount Semeru (East Java).

Smartraveller Indonesia: the revised criminal code includes penalties for cohabitation, adultery and sex outside marriage between a man and a woman; if married, authorities can act on a complaint from a spouse; if unmarried, on a complaint from a child or parent.
Smartraveller Indonesia local emergency contacts: fire 113; ambulance and rescue 118; medical emergencies 119; police 110 or 112 (SMS 1717).

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (updated 18/08/2026): you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is recognised if valid where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law; not recognised where a party is already married, underage, too closely related or forced; some authorities only accept CNIs issued in their own country; talk to a lawyer to confirm validity. Carried over from the Indonesian pack (checked 2026-11-03), NOT re-fetched in this batch.

UNESCO page title 'Indonesian Batik' (re-checked live 2026-11-04), inscribed in 2009 (4.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. UNESCO: 'special varieties are incorporated into celebrations of marriage and pregnancy'; infants are carried in batik slings and the dead are shrouded in funerary batik; designs are drawn with dots and lines of hot wax that resists dye, so the artisan colours selectively; meanings come through 'the symbolic meanings of its colours and designs'. UNESCO tags the element 'Wedding'. It names no specific motif (no truntum, sido mukti).

ABSTRACT ONLY (page meta description read): Siregar et al., 'Literature Review: Batik and Wedding Customs According to Javanese Tradition', ICOMSI 2023 proceedings, Atlantis Press (2024). Batik in traditional Javanese wedding processions is interpreted as hopes and prayers made by the bride and her family for the household; batik motifs are seen as factors that bring goodness. Literature review; motif-level claims not read.

TITLE AND SEARCH SUMMARY ONLY: Pithaloka (2026), 'Kartini Princess of Java Movie Represent the Significance of Batik Truntum as A Symbolic Expression Worn by Parental Figures on the Wedding Day', Journal of Fashion Design and Textiles (DESILLES), Politeknik Kreatif Indonesia (title confirmed live, HTTP 200). A second search snippet (SMUJO journal, 'Study of Javanese philosophical values in Kliwonan batik', not opened) says the bride's and groom's parents wear truntum cloth with a sabuk kemben and sindur, symbolising hope for eternity. Supports only 'truntum is often worn by the parents' as a widely reported custom; no meaning stated as fact. Sido mukti / sido asih: NOT sourced in this batch.

insider_details.detail: The Embassy's CNI jurisdiction splits Java: a Yogyakarta wedding sits with the Embassy in Jakarta, while Solo (Central Java) and East Java sit with the Consulate-General in Surabaya, and Bali with the Consulate-General in Bali; confirm the right mission with the local Civil Registry or KUA before booking travel to collect it.

Because Civil Registry Offices do not normally accept a CNI issued more than 3 months earlier, and non-Muslim couples must lodge notice at least 10 days ahead, the CNI collection and the notice need to sit inside the same short window before the wedding date.

The Embassy says DFAT cannot advise on Indonesian requirements and both partners must hold the same recognised religion; many couples therefore marry legally in Australia and hold the Javanese rites in Java or Bali as a ceremony (offered as an option, not legal advice).

In the palace account the panggih runs gantal throw, foot washing, egg, then tampa kaya and dhahar klimah, and the groom's sungkeman to the Sultan comes straight after the akad; family weddings vary, so agree the running order with both families and whoever leads the rites before the MC script is written.

Paes ageng starts the day before: in the palace account the bride's forehead and nape hair is shaped after siraman to make the paes outline, so the make-up artist or juru paes needs time on the eve, not just the wedding morning.

Mount Merapi (between Central Java and Yogyakarta) and Mount Semeru (East Java) are on Smartraveller's volcano list; build a Plan B for guest transfers and outdoor rites and watch local alerts in the weeks before.
